summary: Defines two CBOR tags for representing IPv4 and IPv6 addresses and prefixes. CBOR is a compact binary data format, and the tags give a standard way to mark a value as an address or a prefix. This avoids each application inventing its own encoding.

plainLanguage.summary: A little sticker on a number that says this is an Internet address, so everyone reads it the same way.

subtitle: Two CBOR tags, 52 and 54, that mark a value as an IPv4 or IPv6 address or prefix.

tldr.problem: Existing CBOR tags 260 and 261 did not say whether bytes were IPv4 or IPv6 except by length, prevented dropping trailing zeros, and tag 261 was not documented well enough to use.
tldr.mechanism: Tag 54 marks IPv6 and tag 52 marks IPv4. Each wraps a byte string (address) or an array (prefix, or address with prefix length), and prefixes drop trailing zero bytes.
tldr.outcome: The new tags are meant to be used in preference to 260 and 261, which IANA has marked as deprecated for IP addresses.

today: RFC 9164 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2021, and the unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. Tags 260 and 261 are marked in the IANA registry as deprecated in favor of 52 and 54 for IP addresses.

sections.title: Why New Address Tags
sections.content:
CBOR is a compact binary data format. RFC 8949 defines common tags, and tags 260 and 261 were later defined in documents listed with IANA, intended for addresses (260) and prefixes (261).

Tag 260 tells IPv6, IPv4 and MAC addresses apart only by the length of the byte string. That makes it impossible, for example, to drop trailing zeros when encoding IP addresses. Tag 261 was not documented well enough for use.

This specification defines tags 54 and 52, which state IPv6 or IPv4 explicitly in the tag number. They should be used in preference to 260 and 261. MAC addresses are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The old sticker only said address, and you had to guess the kind from its length. The new stickers say IPv4 or IPv6 right on them.

sections.title: The Three Forms
sections.content:
Each tag can wrap three shapes of data.

  • Address Format: the tag applied to a byte string, representing one address. Where a prefix is expected, an address means all bits matter, so a /32 for IPv4 and a /128 for IPv6.
  • Prefix Format: the tag applied to an array that starts with an unsigned integer, giving a CIDR-style prefix of that length.
  • Interface Format: the tag applied to an array that starts with a byte string (the full address, always 16 bytes for IPv6 and 4 for IPv4) followed by an unsigned integer, the prefix length.

The Interface Format may have an optional third element, a zone identifier, an integer (interface index) or a text string (interface name). Zone identifiers are strictly local to the node. If there is only an address and a zone, the prefix length may be the CBOR null (0xF6).
sections.plainLanguage: You can label a single house, a whole street, or a house together with its street size. The sticker works for all three.

sections.title: IPv6 and IPv4 Encodings
sections.content:
IANA allocated tag 54 for IPv6, the ASCII code for '6', and tag 52 for IPv4, the ASCII code for '4'. An IPv6 address is a sixteen-byte byte string inside tag 54, and an IPv4 address is a four-byte byte string inside tag 52.

Examples from the RFC:

  • Address: 52(h'c0000201')
  • IPv6 prefix 2001:db8:1234::/48: 54([48, h'20010db81234'])
  • IPv4 prefix 192.0.2.0/24: 52([24, h'c00002'])
  • IPv4 192.0.2.1/24 as an interface: 52([h'c0000201', 24])
  • With zone: 54([h'fe8000000000020202fffffffe030303', 64, 'eth0'])

The address-with-prefix form is told apart from the prefix form only by the order of the array elements. Zone identifiers may be used with any kind of IP address, not just link-local ones.
sections.plainLanguage: The number 54 means a long IPv6 address and 52 means a short IPv4 one. They were picked because they are the letters 6 and 4 in a computer code.

sections.title: Prefix Rules for Encoders and Decoders
sections.content:
A tag is valid if it matches the CDDL rule ip-address-or-prefix and, for prefixes, the rules below. Together with RFC 8949 deterministic encoding rules, this gives deterministic encoding.

An encoder MUST set unused bytes and unused bits in the final byte to zero, then MUST omit any trailing bytes that are all zeros. So 2001:db8:1230::/44 MUST be encoded as 54([44, h'20010db81230']). The number of bytes omitted is unrelated to the prefix length, so 2001:db8::/64 is 54([64, h'20010db8']).

A decoder MUST check that all bits beyond the prefix length are zero and that the byte string does not end in a zero byte. It MUST also handle a prefix length covering more bits than are present, for example ::/128 encoded as 54([128, h'']).

The RFC suggests decoding by starting with 16 (or 4) zero bytes and copying in the bytes that are present.
sections.plainLanguage: Anything after the street part must be blank, and trailing blanks are left off to save space. The reader puts the blanks back.

sections.title: The CDDL Definition
sections.content:
For use with the Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL), the RFC recommends type names in its Figure 1. The tag rules are #6.54(...) and #6.52(...), each accepting an address, an address with prefix, or a prefix.

Addresses are bytes .size 16 (IPv6) or bytes .size 4 (IPv4). Prefix lengths are 0..128 and 0..32. Prefix bytes are at most 16 or 4 bytes long, and the zone identifier is uint / text.
sections.plainLanguage: CDDL is a recipe card that lets a computer check that an address sticker is filled in the right way.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
Applications need to check tag validity before acting on contents, and that must happen before the tag is turned into a platform-specific representation that could hide validity errors. Requiring the bits after the prefix length to be zero also stops a malicious party from using them to carry covert data. Such abuse is caught by validity checking.

IANA allocated tags 54 (IPv6) and 52 (IPv4) from the Specification Required area of the CBOR Tags registry. It also added the note "DEPRECATED in favor of 52 and 54 for IP addresses" to registrations 260 and 261.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the leftover part must be empty, nobody can hide secret messages in it, and a quick check catches anyone who tries.
